results.parameters: At most one cycle per component; no degree bound.
results.assumptions: Unweighted pseudoforest; each vertex initially knows its own degree. One-bit broadcasts suffice; identifiers are unnecessary. Isolated vertices are selected, and both endpoints of a two-vertex component are selected.
results.theorem: Appendix A, Observation A.1 (forest construction); elementary pseudoforest extension proved here
results.summary: The one-round non-leaf rule works on forests and, by the elementary extension below, on pseudoforests.
results.algorithm: Broadcast whether the local degree equals one. Select vertices of degree zero or at least two, and degree-one vertices whose neighbor also has degree one.
results.proofSketch: In a component with at least three vertices, non-leaves dominate. Assign each non-optimum vertex to an adjacent optimum vertex; the resulting disjoint stars use n−OPT edges. A pseudoforest component has at most n edges, so at most OPT edges remain outside the stars. Every non-optimum non-leaf touches a remaining edge, giving at most 2 OPT such vertices, plus at most OPT optimum vertices. Singleton and two-vertex components have ratios one and two. Sum over components.
results.provenanceNote: Folklore non-leaf construction; 2022 identifies the source documenting the forest case, not discovery credit. The broader pseudoforest statement is explicitly derived here.
results.derivationNote: The cited observation states the forest case. The pseudoforest scope is an elementary extension, with the same one-bit protocol and the proof given here; it is not attributed as a separate theorem in that paper.

results.parameters: Δ is the maximum degree; the algorithm need not know it.
results.assumptions: Unweighted graphs. No identifiers, degree knowledge, or communication are needed.
results.summary: Selecting every vertex provides the elementary degree-dependent benchmark.
results.proofSketch: A vertex dominates at most Δ + 1 vertices, so OPT is at least n/(Δ + 1). The output has n vertices.
results.provenanceNote: Folklore baseline documented by the cited source; 2010 is the source year, not a discovery claim.

results.parameters: Integer t ≥ 2; the algorithm need not know t.
results.assumptions: Unweighted. No identifiers, degree knowledge, or communication are needed.
results.summary: The excluded-star condition bounds the cost of selecting all vertices.
results.proofSketch: Excluding K₁,ₜ as a minor implies Δ ≤ t − 1. Thus every optimum vertex dominates at most t vertices, and n ≤ t · OPT.
results.provenanceNote: Folklore baseline documented by the cited source; 2025 is the source year, not a discovery claim.

results.parameters: All vertices have the same positive degree.
results.assumptions: Unweighted regular graphs of positive degree. No identifiers, degree knowledge, or communication are needed.
results.summary: Selecting all vertices is a two-approximation on positive-degree regular graphs.
results.proofSketch: A d-regular graph has dn/2 edges. A vertex cover of size p meets at most dp edges, so OPT ≥ n/2 for d ≥ 1.
results.provenanceNote: Folklore baseline documented by the cited source; 2025 is the source year, not a discovery claim.

results.assumptions: Unweighted. No geometric representation or identifiers are needed. One empty-message round detects isolates; zero rounds suffice if local degree is initially known.
results.summary: Selecting every nonisolated vertex gives a geometry-free constant approximation.
results.algorithm: Send a dummy message on every incident edge, then select vertices that receive a message.
results.proofSketch: Outside an optimum cover, nonisolated vertices form an independent set and each has a neighbor in the cover. A unit-disk neighborhood contains at most five independent neighbors, so at most five such vertices are charged to each optimum vertex. Including the cover itself gives factor six.
results.provenanceNote: Folklore baseline documented by the cited source; 2025 is the source year, not a discovery claim. The one-round isolate detection is an explicit implementation choice.
